newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australian bonds square up for jobs showdown.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australian bonds square up for jobs showdown.

text.p: *Australian bonds ended little changed as a late short squeeze in the run-up to today's U.S. labour force report helped to erode the market's initial U.S.-led fall.
Australian bonds ended little changed as a late short squeeze helped the market recoup their initial U.S. led price fall, traders said.

Trading was relatively light after another volatile trading week, which at one stage saw long-dated bond yields 1/4 point higher than a week ago, being dragged up by repeated weakness in U.S. Treasuries ahead of today's key U.S. labour force report.
"It's the big one tonight, and the risk is the U.S. is going to deteriorate further," one trader added.
The August non-farm payrolls are at 22.30 p.m. (1230 GMT) and are seen rising 244,000 against July's 193,000 increase.

However, some analysts in a Reuters survey were predicting a rise as high as 280,000, a level that could be the final clincher for the Federal Reserve to endorse a policy tightening when the FOMC meets on September 24.
"If we get a strong number, the uncertainty then will be whether it's going to be a 25 or 50 basis point tightening," one trader said.

Locally the aggressive liquidation seen over the past week on Fed hike fears and disappointment of no policy easing here after Tuesday's RBA board meeting has left the market going into the U.S. data neutral and ready to pick up the pieces on Monday.

The late squeeze helped the market reverse an early widening bias in bond yield spreads against both the U.S. and Canada. The market has slowly clawed back some of Tuesday's blow out after the jump in July retail sales, but the 10-year spread to the U.S. remains above Monday's low of around 115 basis points.

The 10-year bond contract held above key support at 91.665/91.670 during the early fall, an area that represents a 38.2 percent retracement of the 90.800 to 92.210 rally seen through June to August, and is also on the line of a one month downward sloping trend. -- Colin Brinsden 61-2 373-1800
